beats.got: The aim is a small, honest checker that says what it cannot catch. I still do not know what a judge file is.

beats.got: That is exactly how I feel when I forward an AI-written summary to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The LLM, left to itself, has no model of truth, only a model of what usually comes next in language that looks like yours.
beats.got: The tool sounds equally sure whether or not the files back it up, so a confident tone says nothing about whether it is right.

beats.trigger: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it
beats.got: Small error rates multiply across a long chain of steps. That worries me for something like onboarding, which has many steps and nobody checking them.

beats.trigger: Round 1: 10% fabricated → 1% after fix.
beats.got: If a check catches most errors and you repeat it, errors shrink fast. But the numbers are made up and the 90% catch rate looks too tidy.

beats.trigger: Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.
beats.got: Asking the AI "are you sure?" is worthless as a check, and I have been doing exactly that.

beats.trigger: Run several candidate methods in parallel and measure which one catches what your benchmark says it should.
beats.got: Do not trust whichever method someone recommends. Try several and measure.

beats.trigger: Does the briefing say more than the sources actually support?
beats.got: There are four kinds of checking. Triangulation, entailment and disconfirmation were used before I knew what they meant, and I only half followed.

beats.trigger: Against the Mata v. Avianca pre-read, source triangulation caught an unsourced "small firm" descriptor and an unsupported "ten minutes" estimate.
beats.got: Each method caught a different kind of error in the lawyer case. Precision and recall are named here but not yet explained.

beats.trigger: Grounded output names what it doesn't know. A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: The checker should state its own blind spots, which is the honest and understated style I trust.

beats.trigger: Grounding is the discipline; fabrication is the failure: invented case law, invented medications, confident numbers nobody can source.
beats.got: Fabrication is the failure and grounding is the habit that prevents it. The examples are vivid but nothing here is about my work.

beats.trigger: Two runs is a demo, not a measurement.
beats.got: Running the same prompt twice shows what wobbles but proves nothing. That is the third technical slide in a row with nobody in it.

beats.trigger: The winner becomes a judge file you carry into Module 6.
beats.got: I will end up with a reusable checker file after about an hour.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: I deliberately produce a briefing with some made-up content so the checkers have something to find. That is odd but logical.

beats.trigger: Why a separate worker? It runs in its own context, so your main session never sees what was fabricated.
beats.got: The part that writes the errors is kept apart from the part that supervises, like a blind trial.

beats.trigger: Thirty is not statistical, but enough to start seeing the pattern.
beats.got: The AI lists thirty claims from the briefing for the checkers to examine. I pasted the prompt and waited.

beats.trigger: Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and its own output file.
beats.got: Four helpers run while I watch. I opened my inbox, because this was the third technical step with no word about who does this work.

beats.trigger: recall (of what the scorer adjudicated as ungrounded, how much did the detector catch?)
beats.got: Precision is how often a flag was right. Recall is how much of the real problem it found. That is the same trade-off as false alarms versus misses when screening CVs.

beats.trigger: You can point at a row and say *this is why I'm keeping this one*.
beats.got: I can defend a choice with a table instead of a reputation, which is what I would want to bring to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: The "known limit" line names what you measured and decided not to chase.
beats.got: I now have a short reusable file that says what it checks and where it stops. I could show it to my HR business partners.

beats.trigger: You chose by measurement, not by reputation.
beats.got: Thirty claims is a demo and real use needs hundreds, but the method stays the same.

beats.trigger: The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.
beats.got: The same four-step pattern should work on other quality questions, maybe including how we screen candidates.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the benchmark and updates the root instructions file with rules for when future sessions run a groundedness check before trusting an output.
beats.got: The AI writes standing rules for when to check, though I am not sure I understand what a root instructions file is.

beats.trigger: Left alone, the agent treats the root instructions file as a clean canvas, so a small edit becomes a full rewrite and your earlier rules drift.
beats.got: You must tell the AI what not to touch, or it rewrites everything, like a new hire reorganising the whole handbook.

beats.trigger: policy claims in internal advice
beats.got: The riskiest outputs are the ones that get repeated, and wrong policy answers are on that list. That is an HR problem, and I am supposed to argue with the summary.

beats.trigger: the agent proposes the action, you quality-check the proposal against the judge or the source, then it applies.
beats.got: The AI proposes, a person checks, and then it acts. At last a human has a role in the loop.

beats.trigger: The expert reviews the proposed action, the evidence behind it, and the known limit of the check that passed it.
beats.got: Someone expert must own the review. That raises my question about who in my organisation that is and how they learn it.

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a source; accurate is harder.
beats.got: A grounded claim has a source, which is not the same as being true. Fair summary.

beats.trigger: Once the judge and pre-read are ready, end this session.
beats.got: One more reading, then a fresh session for the next module.

beats.trigger: Evals scale it to three hundred claims, run the judge on every build, and feed its feedback into generation between rounds.
beats.got: This scales up to a bigger version run automatically, but "build" and "generation" are engineer language and I lost the thread.

take_homes: Asking the AI "are you sure?" proves nothing. A confident tone is not evidence, so something outside the model has to check.
Do not pick a quality check by reputation. Try a few on my own material, read the scoreboard and keep the one I can defend, including what it misses.
A person still reviews the proposal before the agent acts, and that reviewer needs to be an expert. I have to work out who that is in my organisation.

monday.move: Take my weekly people-metrics summary draft and ask a second agent to check each number against the HR system export. Write down what that check cannot catch, and bring the results to one HR partner.
monday.who: Me and one HR business partner, using only aggregate numbers.
monday.stop_condition: Stop if the check needs employee-level data before I have asked the DPO and the works council.
monday.blocker: I have not yet asked the DPO or the works council about employee data in an AI tool.

misconception.why: The module never discussed headcount. The human-in-the-loop expert hinted that roles shift toward review rather than disappear, but nothing in it answered which roles go, so I still expect headcount questions first.

one_line: The scoreboard idea is useful, and the 'are you sure?' point is worth the hour, but it is written for engineers and says almost nothing about the people who will check the work.
